canberra.title: Bird flu hits Merimbula, wetlands committee on alert
canberra.snippet: H5 bird flu has been detected in two crested terns at Spencer Park and Mitchies Jetty, Merimbula, following testing conducted over the we...
canberra.content:
Bird flu has been detected at Mitchies Jetty, Merimbula. Photo: Denise Dion.

H5 bird flu has been detected in two crested terns at Spencer Park and Mitchies Jetty, Merimbula, following testing conducted over the weekend.

The NSW Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) H5 Bird Flu Incident Management Team confirmed the birds tested positive for H5 avian influenza.

Keen bird watcher Robyn Kesby is on the Panboola Wetlands committee and is a member of the Far South Coast Bird Watchers.

“I’ve had the hotline on my phone for a couple of years now,” Ms Kesby said.

There’s a sense of resignation as she said they had been advised about what to do and had anticipated that the H5 bird flu would inevitably come to the area.

“It’s very early days and we’re not sure how it will travel outside the coastal areas. The crested terns nest and travel in dense flocks and this makes them more susceptible,” she said.

“There’s been concern about the penguins at Eden. We had a meeting of the Far South Coast Birdwatchers recently where seabird researcher Nicholas Carlisle spoke and was asked about the Eden penguins. But it’s a small colony and they’re not nesting so closely together and we think they are less susceptible,” Ms Kesby said.

She urged everyone to have the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on their phone and to follow government advice to avoid contact and report a sighting as quickly as possible.

“Keep yourselves safe, avoid coming into contact with dead or injured birds and keep your dog on a lead,” Ms Kesby said.

Panboola Wetlands. Photo: Denise Dion.

Panboola Wetlands. Photo: Denise Dion.

Panboola Wetland. Photo: Denise Dion.

“Take a photo and send it to the hotline. Anyone reporting a sick or dead bird will be given a report number and then the job is allocated for checking and removal for testing.”

Local agencies, including the NSW Local Land Services, National Parks and Wildlife Service and Bega Valley Shire Council are working together to monitor and respond to reports.

Advisory signage has been installed at both locations to remind the community to avoid contact with sick or dead birds and marine animals. The number of reports to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline and the number of birds and marine mammals being tested locally are increasing.

Ms Kesby said they were monitoring the situation at Panboola Wetlands, the popular walking and birdwatching site. She urged members of the public to contact the hotline first with any reports of sick or dead bird and then to let Panboola know through the Facebook page or leave a message on 0414 864 873.

“We are being vigilant and we are concerned but we have to wait and see what happens. We can hope there’s some resistance but we don’t know how many of each species will be affected,” Ms Kesby said.

At this stage, H5 bird flu has not been detected in commercial poultry flocks or captive birds anywhere in Australia.

There is also currently no evidence of mass mortality in wildlife or spread to other animals and pets in NSW, and the risk to human health remains low.

Signs of H5 bird flu in birds can include:

  • sudden death without clinical signs, including mass mortality events
  • lethargy or reluctance to walk, eat or drink
  • a droopy appearance or ruffled feathers
  • neurological signs such as tremors, poor coordination, unusual postures, inability to walk or stand, or seizures
  • respiratory signs such as panting, nasal discharge, coughing or sneezing
  • swelling around the head and neck
  • watery or green diarrhoea.

In poultry, signs may also include a sudden decrease in egg production and purple discolouration or bruising of the wattles, combs and legs.

Infected wild mammals can show a range of signs, including neurological symptoms such as paralysis, seizures and tremors, respiratory signs and sudden death, including potentially mass mortality events.

If you find a sick or dead animal, do not touch it.

Instead:

  1. Record the location and number of affected animals and, if it is safe to do so, take photographs.
  2. Report the sighting by calling the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888.
  3. After calling the hotline, reports can also be made through the Snap Send Solve app using the category Animal – Suspected Bird Flu. This allows people to attach photographs and mark the location.

More information

NSW information about H5 bird flu, including advice for livestock, backyard birds and pets, is available from the NSW Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development.

National updates and information about bird flu are available from the Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry.

Original Article published by Denise Dion on About Regional.

canberra.title: Should the proposed coercive control penalty be lowered to prevent manipulation by defendants?
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to family violence. The suggested maximum penalty for a standalone coercive control offence could re...
canberra.content:
The debate about the best way to criminalise coercive control in the ACT continues, as stakeholders differ on the appropriate maximum penalty, the definition of relationships and whether the fault element should be recklessness or intent. Photo: Marisa Paterson MLA.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to family violence.

The suggested maximum penalty for a standalone coercive control offence could result in accused perpetrators using the system to extend their power over their alleged victims, a committee inquiry has heard.

The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) raised this concern during the steering committee consultation, given section 374 of the Crimes Act 1900 only allows the prosecution to decide if a matter can stay in the Magistrates Court (and hence not be heard by a jury) for offences punishable by imprisonment for longer than two years but shorter than five years.

The proposed coercive control legislation outlines a maximum penalty of seven years for the offence.

Domestic and family violence sector representatives have expressed concerns that this will allow coercive control perpetrators to keep exerting power over their victims.

“Perpetrators of domestic and family violence are often adept at manipulating systems to extend their control,” YWCA Canberra submitted to a committee inquiry into the proposed legislation.

“Where [defendant] consent is required for summary disposal [ie, keeping the case in the lower court], there is a real risk that individuals accused of coercive control will elect the Supreme Court where longer wait times will prolong proceedings and extend the period during which victim-survivors remain exposed to ongoing harm.”

This can result in delays of more than a year – and even up to three years – of a person’s case.

The Women’s Legal Centre submitted systemic delays in the Supreme Court proceedings would “require victim-survivors to participate in lengthy indictable proceedings and expose them to prolonged uncertainty, repeated engagement with the criminal justice system and an increased risk of retraumatisation”.

However, these groups still support the seven-year maximum penalty.

Instead, it has been suggested that a carve-out be created in the law to still allow the prosecution to prevent a case from being sent to the higher court.

“As ACT Policing has observed, the proposed maximum penalty would provide access to a broader range of investigative powers that may assist in the effective investigation of these complex offences,” the Women’s Legal Centre submitted.

“[We recommend] that the proposed maximum penalty of seven years’ imprisonment be retained to reflect the seriousness of coercive control and its strong association with domestic homicide; and [that] the Bill be amended to create a specific legislative exception permitting coercive control offences to be heard summarily in appropriate circumstances.”

The ACT Law Society rejects a carve-out.

Representative Adrian McKenna told the inquiry hearings it wouldn’t be appropriate to “make this the only crime in the Territory that has a special prosecution power for the [DPP]”.

“Is the balance to have the toughest, so to speak, maximum penalty for the offence possible, or to balance that against the risk of having matters dragged through the Supreme Court?” he argued.

“It is possible for a prosecution to persuade a magistrate to stop a defendant misusing the system and committing the matter for trial. [But] the concern is that that does not often happen.”

Steering Committee member Claire Buxton, who is also the Justice and Community Safety Directorate executive branch manager of legislation, policy and programs, told the inquiry the seven-year maximum penalty was landed on in part as it was commensurate to other like-offences in the legislation.

Prevention of Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Minister Caitlin Tough said it was about recognising the seriousness and harm caused by such offending.

“We’re showing [coercive control] is not a small thing,” she said.

But a word of warning was given by a victim-survivor.

“Anything that has the risk of handing more control to someone who’s using coercive control is something that should be thought through really carefully,” she told the hearings.

It’s one of many issues with the proposed legislation aired during the committee inquiry’s hearings.

Other concerns included the broad definition of which relationships could be captured by the law, and whether proving intent to harm (rather than recklessness) was too high a threshold to meet.

The committee inquiry into the proposed coercive control offence continues.

Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 02 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 02 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. canberra.title: New charges laid against church group member accused of abusing children
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse. A former member of Canberra church groups is facing a growing list of charge...
canberra.content:
Toby Charles Mortlock, 60, faces numerous charges in the ACT Supreme and Magistrates Courts. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse.

A former member of Canberra church groups is facing a growing list of charges relating to the alleged historical sexual abuse of multiple children in the ACT.

Toby Charles Mortlock, now aged 60, has been accused of abusing eight children in the 1980s and 1990s when the children were all of primary school age.

The total number of charges he faces, as well as their details, were not immediately clear because some have already been committed to the ACT Supreme Court while others are still progressing before the ACT Magistrates Court.

But on Thursday (20 August), the lower court heard he had been handed an additional four counts of committing an act of indecency on a person under 10, which were on top of his previous charges.

Mr Mortlock’s lawyer, Legal Aid’s Duncan Errey, said his client had been issued his charges via summons, which meant he was not required to face court in person. He entered not guilty pleas on his client’s behalf.

When Special Magistrate Lucinda Wilson said Mr Mortlock would be required to attend court in person on the next occasion if his matter was to be committed, Mr Errey asked that he appear in court via audio-visual link.

The special magistrate questioned why he should be allowed to when he lived in NSW but was close to the ACT.

Prosecutor James Melloy said his office was aware that Mr Mortlock had difficulties travelling, so did not oppose him appearing in court via an audio-visual link.

The matter was adjourned to 29 October.

Mr Mortlock’s charges in the Magistrate Court now include 19 counts of committing an act of indecency on a person under 10, two counts each of sexual intercourse with a person under 10 and assault, as well as one count of sexual intercourse with a person under 16.

He previously entered not guilty pleas to the charges in the Supreme Court and is set to face trial on these counts.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said Mr Mortlock had been known to frequent multiple church groups and regularly attended church community events in Canberra.

“[He] also held roles at a High Commission, as an after-school care worker and as a swimming instructor,” a police spokesperson previously said.

Police said he had been connected to the following places in the 1980s and 1990s: Tuggeranong Alliance Church in Wanniassa, The Fairy Garden in Tuggeranong, City Mission Church in Civic, O’Connor Uniting Church in O’Connor and Capital Christian Church in Phillip.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 02 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 02 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

canberra.title: WATCH: Allegedly dangerous driving teen caught after fleeing police
canberra.snippet: Police are asking for witnesses to come forward after they caught an alleged dangerous driver and his two passengers while they were tryi...
canberra.content:
20 August 2026

20 August 2026

An 18-year-old man has been arrested after he was allegedly filmed driving dangerously through Giralang on 16 August 2026 before trying to run away from officers. Video: ACT Policing.

Police are asking for witnesses to come forward after they caught an alleged dangerous driver and his two passengers while they were trying to flee officers.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said officers spotted a silver Ford Falcon being driven without number plates on Gundaroo Drive in the Belconnen suburb of Giralang at around 4:30 pm on Sunday (16 August).

It is alleged the car was being driven dangerously, including speeding, weaving through traffic and performing burnouts at roundabouts.

While police deployed tyre deflation devices and directed the driver to stop, he allegedly refused to comply, sparking a car chase.

The Ford was driven on damaged tyres before stopping in a greenbelt. While the driver, alleged to be an 18-year-old man from Holt, and his two passengers tried to run from the scene, they were soon caught by police.

The 18-year-old has been scheduled to face the ACT Magistrates Court in October charged with furious/reckless/dangerous driving, failing to stop for police, using an unregistered vehicle, using an uninsured vehicle and trespassing.

The police spokesperson said anyone who witnessed the alleged incident and has not yet spoken with officers should contact Crime Stoppers. Quote reference number 8473458.

canberra.title: Catholic school parents face fees shake-up
canberra.snippet: Catholic school parents are being prepared for a shake-up in fees as the system plans for growth, including a new co-ed school in Canberr...
canberra.content:
Catholic Education Canberra and Goulburn is facing funding pressures. Photo: CECG.

Catholic school parents are being prepared for a shake-up in fees as the system plans for growth, including a new co-ed school in Canberra’s south, aims to make fees fairer, and braces for looming changes to Commonwealth funding.

Catholic Education Canberra and Goulburn Executive Director David de Carvalho told a gathering at the National Convention Centre for the launch of its 10-year Apostolic Action Plan on Thursday (20 August) that the goal was 25 per cent growth in capacity to cater for 30,000 students across the archdiocese, up from 24,000.

That would include upgrades and new schools, such as more co-ed secondary schooling options on the south side of Canberra.

The challenge would be finding the money to pay for this while remaining committed to being accessible to all families wanting a Catholic education.

Mr de Carvalho said that without more government funding, there would be pressure on fees, so there would need to be a change in how they were structured to ensure they remained fair and took into account families’ capacity to pay.

This would occur from 2028 and reflect the different circumstances of school communities.

Speaking to Region before the launch, Mr de Carvalho said this meant the uniform fee structure for primary school students across the system instituted over the past five years would be replaced by one that acknowledged a school community’s means.

That would mean wealthier school communities would pay more than families in less well-off schools.

CECG executive director David de Carvalho says that from 2028 fees will differ across the archdiocese. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

“Wealthier communities are being cross-subsidised by the poorer communities, and it’s inconsistent with the way the Commonwealth funds schools by looking at capacity to contribute,” he said.

“So we’re going to have to start rethinking how we set our fee structure in a way that reflects government policy more accurately.

“And to be fair, that principle that the government uses, there’s some social justice thinking behind it.”

Mr de Carvalho said parents would be given plenty of time to adjust to the early rollout of the fees schedule next year, before the usual Term 3 announcement.

He said school planning and financial sustainability were two tandem projects in train to address the need to spend a lot of money on school upgrades and expansion, and the uncertainty around Commonwealth funding.

All schools had been audited, and demographic trends looked at to identify what work needed to be done and where demand was greatest.

Mr de Carvalho said the absence of a co-ed campus on the southside of Canberra was a huge issue.

“All we’ve got is MacKillop down the end, and on the northside we’ve got two – St Francis Xavier and John-Paul II – and there’s this kind of missing middle,” he said.

There are plans for more Early Learning Centre areas such as Batemans Bay and Yass, and to offer a seamless transition between ELCs and primary schools.

CECC will also develop a masterplan for growth areas such as Goulburn and Queanbeyan, and explore extending St Patrick’s Parish School in Cooma to Years 11 and 12.

Mr de Carvalho said the Commonwealth’s Choice and Affordability Fund, which is helping the non-government school system transition to the new Gonski funding model, would run out in 2029.

“So the question is, what does the non-government funding system look like from 2030 on?” he said.

“We need to get our house in order.”

australia.title: Zomi Frankcom deserved more, slain aid worker’s family says, after Israel rejects criminal investigation
australia.snippet: In strongly worded statement, family says IDF announcement an ‘insult’ to Australian woman’s memory The family of the slain Australian ai...
australia.content:
The family of the slain Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom has described a decision by the Israel Defense Forces not to open a criminal investigation into her death as deeply disappointing, and called on the government to push for the release of evidence, including audio from the drone strike.

Israel’s decision prompted outrage from Australia on Thursday. The country’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, was called in by the foreign affairs minister Penny Wong, while the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, expressed “outrage” and insisted he would press for justice for Frankcom and her colleagues.

The April 2024 strike hit a convoy of World Central Kitchen vehicles, killing seven employees of the US-based aid group, which has distributed food in Gaza throughout the war.

The group had coordinated with the Israeli military over the movement of its convoy. But its vehicles were left incinerated and mangled after being repeatedly struck.

“This was not a single, instantaneous strike,” Frankcom’s family said in a statement.

“Three clearly marked humanitarian vehicles traveling in a humanitarian fire control zone were struck successively as survivors attempted to move from one vehicle to another.”

The family took exception to the announcement on World Humanitarian Day, which commemorates workers killed while helping others.

Frankcom’s family had attended an event with Wong only hours earlier, announcing a humanitarian award in Zomi’s name.

They said the timing of the announcement was “an insult” to her memory.

“Zomi and her colleagues deserve more than an internal, opaque process that ends with a short statement by the Israeli Military absolving their soldiers of criminal wrongdoing.”

They called on Labor to demand full disclosure of the evidence used by Israel and an acknowledgement that the high-level military officer involved in the strikes had been one of 130 signatories to a January 2024 letter calling for a block on aid to Gaza.

“We also call on the Australian government to pursue all available legal avenues for an independent and credible investigation to be conducted.”

The IDF said on Wednesday it had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the convoy deviated from the previously coordinated route.

It concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded.

Wong said she had told Newman “that Israel’s decision falls far short of the accountability we expect.”

“Democracies seek and accept higher standards,” Wong said. “The Australian government will continue to keep pressing Israel for justice for Zomi and her colleagues and we will consult with Zomi Frankcom’s family before we announce further steps.”

She conceded it was a “difficult time in the relationship” with Israel.

In question time in Canberra, the prime minister said Israel’s decision was “an outrage”.

“Since the tragic killings, the government has consistently made clear our expectation for transparency, and we’ve pressed for full accountability,” Albanese said.

“The Australian government will not stop pressing Israel for justice for Ms Frankcom and her colleagues.”

Newman said the investigators had found no criminal liability by the soldiers involved, but refused to apologise for the deaths, saying such a move would bring legal ramifications.

“A court came to a decision that there’s no criminal liability, so we’re not going to lynch people on the streets, no.”

“There were mistakes made by the convoy, but there were mistakes made by Israel.”

Opposition frontbencher James Paterson said Frankcom “never should have been killed.”

“It’s a tragedy that she was, and it is incredibly concerning to hear this news out of Israel,” he said.

australia.title: Australia news live: NSW police commissioner says ‘I unreservedly apologise’ for miscommunication over 18-year-old bushwalker Lily Hooper’s death
australia.snippet: Follow today’s news live Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast ‘Outrageous’: Greens leader says sending Israeli am...
australia.content:
NSW police apologise for miscommunication over Lily Hooper’s death

The NSW police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, has apologised for a miscommunication that led to inaccurate initial reports that missing 18-year-old bushwalker Lily Hooper had been found alive.

Within 10 minutes, the search crew relayed a “more accurate account” to police, confirming that Hooper had died.

Speaking to reporters, Lanyon says:

I unreservedly apologise for any additional trauma that may have caused Lily’s family, and certainly for the embarrassment and confusion it caused.

The miscommunication was obviously born out of elation that Lily had been found. Her condition at that time was understood to be such that searchers were relieved, and those at the command post were elated.

Tragically, that miscommunication then led to a deflation, and we now know it had an impact on her family. Once again, I unreservedly apologise for that miscommunication.

    Welcome

What we learned today, Thursday 20 August

Another jam-packed news day!

Before we shut this blog, let’s recap what the top headlines were:

  • The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said the government was “outraged” over the decision by the Israel Defense Forces not to pursue a criminal investigation into the strike on an aid convoy in 2024 that killed seven people, including Australian Zomi Frankcom.

  • After a meeting with Wong, Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, backed the IDF’s decision and refused to apologise over Frankcom’s death.

  • The body of 18-year-old Lily Hooper who went missing last week has been found. It came after a major miscommunication that the NSW police has apologised for.

  • The eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, did the media rounds this morning, after putting Roblox, which has been accused of hosting grooming and sexual exploitation on its platform, on notice to improve its safety measures or face court.

  • The government’s gambling reforms passed the Senate late last night after hours of debate, bringing in new restrictions to limit gambling advertising and a one-stop “opt-out register”.

  • The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, formally called for a royal commission into alleged corruption in the construction sector.

  • Australia’s Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander social justice commissioner, Katie Kiss, has told the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion that Australia will not be able to address racism towards any other community that has settled in this country until it deals with its racism towards First Peoples.

  • The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, has declared a “significant escalation” in H5 bird flu in the state after the detection of three mass mortality events involving more than 1,000 greater crested terns.

  • Separately, the Tasmanian government said it was investigating 28 little penguin deaths on King Island with testing under way to determine whether the birds died of H5 bird flu.

  • For those who missed it, here’s a tl;dr on what happened in question time.

Thanks for sticking around, we’ll be back tomorrow morning.

Josh Taylor

More than 60 Victorian day cares shuttered over child safety risks

Sixty-five family day care residences have been ordered to close across Victoria for 90 days after the state regulator suspended childcare company Ignite Minds and four educators over alleged serious breaches of national regulations it says created risks to the safety of children.

The Victorian Early Childhood Regulatory Authority (Vecra) and the federal education department inspected 30 residences operated by Ignite Minds, code-named Operation Flint, to assess compliance.

Vecra said its officers “directly observed evidence of harms and hazards” that posed “serious risks” to child safety.

The company has been ordered to immediately close all 65 family day care residences for 90 days while the alleged breaches are addressed.

Ignite Minds has been directed to notify parents and carers of the suspension.

In a statement on Thursday, Ignite Minds said it treats the safety and wellbeing of children “with the utmost seriousness” and acknowledged there had been some compliance deficiencies at some of the 30 locations inspected.

However, the company said immediate action was taken where concerns were raised and Ignite Minds “strongly dispute[s] the necessity of the immediate, blanket suspension”. The company said:

We believe this disproportionate action disrupts care across our network and does not serve the interests of the children or the families who form this wonderful community.

We are actively working through our options to address these allegations and are cooperating with the regulator.

We are particularly concerned that this suspension was issued while Ignite Minds was already in the process of submitting evidence of rectification and compliance.

Ignite Minds operates across metropolitan Melbourne, as well as in Bendigo, Shepparton and Elphinstone.

Family day care residences are run by educators in their own home for education of children typically up to 12 years old.

Four individual educators have also been suspended, as Vecra said they pose a risk to children’s safety.

Other alleged breaches included children leaving a property unsupervised, and a child falling from a high chair. Vecra also said there were unsafe environments, with dangers and hazards including poisons and chemicals, beehives, and inadequate fencing.

The company also did not provide adequate care for children with medical conditions, Vecra claimed, including maintaining health plans, and the provision of medication on-site.

The Victorian early childhood regulator, Wendy Steendam, said she was aware suspending the provider would affect childcare arrangements, but the decision was made “because we know they [families] wouldn’t want us to compromise on safety”. She said in a statement:

Family day care providers are on notice. You must ensure your educators and their residences are compliant, and you must provide appropriate governance and leadership to your staff. If you don’t, we will act.

Ignite Minds said standard regulatory practice was to collaborate with providers to “resolve issues before resorting to public allegations”.

Ignite Minds said:

We recognise that this news may be distressing, and we are truly sorry for the uncertainty it causes our families.

An emergency action notice was issued after a five-month-old child was observed sleeping in a cot with what Vecra described as items that “posed an immediate risk to their safety and wellbeing”.

Council hopes IDF investigation decision brings closure after ‘devastating tragedy’

The Australia/Israel & Jewish Affairs Council (AIJAC) said it hoped the IDF’s decision to close its investigation into the killings of aid workers would bring “closure” to “a devastating tragedy”.

In a statement, the executive director, Dr Colin Rubenstein, said:

The death of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom and her six World Central Kitchen colleagues in Gaza was profoundly tragic.

Regrettably, errors are an inevitable part of warfare, particularly given the complexity of urban warfare against a terror group such as Hamas. The WCK incident was a particularly tragic example. Yet what matters is how militaries in a democracy respond.

We hope the Israeli investigation’s final findings – which, as noted, are fully consistent with Australia’s own investigations – can bring some closure following that terrible error.

Continuing on the police commissioner’s press conference, Mal Lanyon says an investigation into the incident and broader communication procedures has been launched:

We’ll look at the relationship between police and the SES and we’ll work with other agencies to make sure communication failures don’t occur.

Communication is always a challenge, and in remote areas from time to time it can be challenging to get the right communication through. We want to make sure it’s as simple as possible.

Speaking to reporters, Lanyon says:

The miscommunication was obviously born out of elation that Lily had been found. Her condition at that time was understood to be such that searchers were relieved, and those at the command post were elated.

Outrage ‘hasn’t materialised into action’: Faruqi calls for consequences against Israel

The Greens deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi, has accused the government of failing to take meaningful action over Israel’s decision not to pursue a criminal investigation into the 2024 strike that killed Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom and six other humanitarian workers.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Faruqi said:

Israel today has abrogated all responsibility and accountability for their murder. Of course, the prime minister, the foreign minister and everyone else should be outraged. But they were outraged more than two years ago when these murders took place. It’s been years since then, and that outrage, again and again, hasn’t materialised into any action or accountability.

She called on the government to impose stronger consequences against Israel, saying:

We could have had an independent investigation. We could have referred this murder to the ICC, which is what the World Central Kitchen was asking for at the time.

We could have sanctioned Israel. We could have expelled the Israeli ambassador. There should have been some consequences for the murder of an Australian citizen and an incredible aid worker who was committed to humanity and working in the most difficult conditions. None of those actions were taken.

For a lot of people in this country, outrage is merely words that mean nothing.

Krishani Dhanji

Thank you all so much for following along on the blog with me this sitting fortnight!

I’ll leave you with the fabulous Achol Arok. Take care.

Josh Butler

News bargaining incentive backed by News Corp

News Corp has welcomed the passage of the news bargaining incentive, calling it “much-needed investment” for the journalism sector.

As Krishani brought you earlier, the NBI – which obligates big tech companies to make commercial deals with at least six media outlets, to support journalism – passed parliament earlier, among a rush of legislation pushed through both houses this week.

“Australian news organisations now get the much-needed investment to continue delivering professional journalism vital to our democracy and local communities,” said Michael Miller, the executive chair of News Corp Australia.

This again shows the Australian Government’s willingness to be a world leader in developing policies that benefit everyday Australians and the public interest.

Meta, TikTok and Google will have to sign deals with media outlets under the new rules, or pay a higher levy which would be distributed by the government.

Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

  • Matt Keogh again copped multiple questions on a controversial cap on allied health services for veterans (which Jacqui Lambie blasted the government for in the Senate yesterday).

  • The Coalition again called for Keogh to be sacked, quoting one veteran who said they would prefer to “deal with the Taliban” over the veterans’ affairs minister.

  • Jim Chalmers also faced a few questions over the budget hitting $1tn of gross debt, which the treasurer tried to throw back at the opposition, saying much of it was accrued under them.

  • Albanese said the government would “not stop pressing Israel for justice” when asked by the independent MP Sophie Scamps what more the government would do, and whether Labor would expel the Israeli ambassador.

  • Zali Steggall asked the government what more it was doing to combat violence against women and children. Anthony Albanese said he would raise the issue at national cabinet next week.

  • And there were three MPs yeeted today – Labor MPs Matt Burnell and Julian Hill and the Liberal frontbencher Tony Pasin.

After a final dixer to Clare O’Neil, Anthony Albanese calls time on QT.

Someone from the opposition bench says “a bit early!” to which Albanese replies, “really?!”

That’s the last question time of the sitting fortnight.

Dan Tehan has a bit of a crack at the PM:

It’s been the normal practice at question time that there’s 20 questions usually asked. Yet what’s happened because we’ve got someone under witness protection …

He gets cut off. And then everyone moves on.

Albanese calls Zomi Frankcom decision 'an outrage'

Will the government expel the Israeli ambassador and what will the government do to ensure justice is served, asks the independent MP Sophie Scamps.

Anthony Albanese says he and the foreign minister, Penny Wong, have consistently called for accountability and transparency from the Israeli government over the killing of Gaza aid workers including Zomi Frankcom.

He also calls the decision not to pursue criminal proceedings an “outrage”.

Israel’s decision to close their investigation without criminal proceedings is an outrage and it falls far short of the accountability that we expect and consistently called for on behalf of Australia. Since the tragic killings, the government has consistently made clear our expectation for transparency, and we’ve pressed for full accountability.

The foreign minister has called in Israel’s ambassador to Australia to strongly register our views, and Australia’s ambassador to Israel has done the same. The Australian government will not stop pressing Israel for justice for Ms Frankcom and her colleagues.

He doesn’t say whether the government will expel the ambassador, but earlier during her press conference, Wong said removing an ambassador “would remove our ability to be able to engage, press for Australia’s interests”.

‘I prefer to deal with the Taliban’: Coalition piles pressure on Keogh

Phil Thompson next asks the prime minister “how much more evidence is needed before you sack this incompetent minister”, and says one veteran told him “I prefer to deal with the Taliban” than Matt Keogh.

The assistant minister Julian Hill is booted by Milton Dick at the end of the question – on his way out he drops his folder.

Anthony Albanese calls that an “unfortunate quote” and defends his minister.

We have responded constructively to the recommendations of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide. That is why we engaged constructively. I met some of the veterans who were here earlier this week, just in the corridor, introduced myself to them. I’ve said I’m happy to meet with them.

Albanese says he will raise combating family and domestic violence at national cabinet next week

Back to QT, independent MP Zali Steggall asks what else the government is going to do to help keep women and children and safe after the recent deaths of women allegedly at the hands of a partner, and multiple high profile sexual assault allegations.

Anthony Albanese says there must be zero tolerance of sexual violence in Australia.

He says next week he will convene national cabinet next week and has put domestic violence on the agenda.

State governments have primary responsibility in areas such as community services ministers, and in those services of the 500 additional workers that we have funded as part of a commitment I took to the 2022 election, that are making a difference on the ground. But that took longer than we would like, frankly, for it to be rolled out. We are seeing, tragically as well, I want to hold governments to account that sometimes when the commonwealth provides additional money, that’s seen as an excuse to withdraw funding … I will raise that very directly with the premiers.

More than 1,000 crested terns found dead with suspected H5 bird flu in three mass mortality events in South Australia

Lisa Cox

Breaking out of question time for a moment:

The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, has declared a “significant escalation” in H5 bird flu in the state after the detection of three mass mortality events involving more than 1,000 crested terns.

State authorities are also investigating a suspected case in a little penguin found on Kangaroo Island, with Malinauskas telling the parliament the development was “of particular concern”.

Malinauskas said aerial surveillance on Wednesday detected the three mass mortality events, all on remote islands. He said more than 1,000 dead crested terns were found across Troubridge Island off the Yorke Peninsula and the Pages Islands (known as North Page and South Page) off Kangaroo Island.

He said the cause of the deaths was presumed to be H5 bird flu.

Malinauskas said:

The loss of more than 1,000 birds is deeply concerning, and the state government is treating these events with the utmost seriousness.

Liberal MP accuses Keogh of ‘gaslighting’ women veterans

Liberal MP Melissa Price has kept the spotlight on Matt Keogh, asking why he has delayed the release of a women’s veteran strategy, and accuses him of “gaslighting” women veterans.

Keogh says that his department has been working on a women’s strategy and has been consulting with veterans and serving personnel, but it’s “been complex work”.

One of the issues that has come up over the time that I have been in the portfolio has been the very real concern expressed by many women veterans about making sure that a system that understandably has been designed primarily over the last century to support male members in the Defence Force.

He hasn’t provide a timeline as to when the work will be delivered.

Dan Tehan stands up to make a point of order, but as he approaches the despatch box, Keogh walks away, indicating he’s finished his answer.

Minister says allied health cap for veterans responds to royal commission recommendations

Michael McCormack is back at the despatch box, and says not one of the 122 recommendations made by the royal commission into defence and veterans’ suicides called for a cap on allied health services.

Matt Keogh says the changes to allied health service access does respond to the recommendations of the royal commission, by increasing the fees for allied health professionals:

One of the things that this measure delivers on is increasing the fees that are going to be paid to allied health service professionals across Australia, recognising the real need that has been spoken about for so long by those providers and by the veteran community. And that was something that was highlighted in recommendation 71.

australia.title: Alan Jones’s ‘yelling stopped’ when his ‘sexual behaviour’ began, alleged victim tells court
australia.snippet: Sydney court hears complainant was more than 40 years younger and far less powerful than the shock jock when he started working as his dr...
australia.content:
Alan Jones’s yelling stopped when his “sexual behaviour” began, the broadcaster’s former driver has alleged.

Complainant C told a Sydney court on Thursday that he had been “reprimanded, yelled at and intimidated” when he worked for the former 2GB host as a young man in the mid-2000s.

But after Jones started touching him on the penis and kissing him, the situation changed, the court heard.

“Once the sexual behaviour began, he was nicer to me,” C told Downing Centre local court during his re-examination.

“I was obviously intimidated, but the yelling stopped.”

The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 20 indecent assault charges and two counts of sexual touching in relation to six men.

Asked why C did not try to stop Jones from kissing him in the lifts at work and at the radio host’s Macquarie Street home, he said he could not.

“There is no circumstance I ever would have pushed Alan away given the power dynamic between us, given my role working for him, given the person he was in my life,” he said.

“He was my boss, he was my employer … and he was a very influential person in our industry.

“I couldn’t resist, I couldn’t say no.”

Years after he stopped working as Jones’s driver, C and the radio host continued to text each other.

After Jones announced his retirement in 2020, C said in a text message that he owed his career to the veteran broadcaster and that he had “only ever treated me with great decency” while his “generosity and kindness towards me has never wavered”.

The defence suggested he could have simply congratulated Jones and said nothing more, but C told the court he was “groomed to write in that manner”.

Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC said: “Grooming is something that happens to young children … He never groomed you.”

C replied: “Grooming is a secretive behaviour that makes you feel you need to act in a certain way, and you are taught to act in a certain way.

“[The grooming] used to happen because he used to touch me on the penis.”

The former driver noted Jones was more than 40 years older than him when he started working for him and held vastly more influence and power than a junior staffer.

“Sending a message like that is like paying tribute,” C said.

“If I didn’t, he wouldn’t have liked it. It would have blown back on me at some point in the future that I was ungrateful.”

Earlier in the week C explained other text messages to Jones with intimate and sexual content were the result of grooming. “These are messages consistent with someone who had been groomed for 10 years to think this was an acceptable way to talk with him,” the complainant said on Tuesday.

It is the defence case that it is “inconsistent” that C would text Jones in an explicit manner if the defendant had indecently assaulted him.

Bashir, who signalled in her opening statement that the charges arose in part as a result of rivalry between Jones and fellow shock jock Ray Hadley, suggested to C that Hadley had been chasing Jones’s breakfast slot in 2019 when he put him in contact with a journalist.

Bashir said Jones was “under pressure” at the time C told Sydney Morning Herald journalist Peter FitzSimons he had been indecently assaulted by his former boss.

C, who spoke to FitzSimons anonymously, told the court he did not want his story to be told at that time, nor did he want to be identified.

“It terrified me. For my own welfare, I couldn’t do it,” he said.

Asked what terrified him by crown prosecutor Georgina Wright SC, C replied: “The repercussions from Alan.”

He said he only wanted FitzSimons to know the behaviour the journalist was investigating was true.

Bashir asked if he was aware that Jones was under pressure at the time due to a social media campaign against the broadcaster by Mad Fucking Witches and a group called the Sleeping Giants; C said it was “because he said something stupid on air”.

He also said he never thought Jones and Hadley were rivals.

“I knew they didn’t like each other but the word ‘rivals’ is not a word I would have used,” he said.

In late 2019, Jones sent a text message to C saying, “I hope you can understand my profound disappointment at the treachery I have endured over the last 18 months.

“Fortunately I know all the players … for you to be involved I find unbelievable.”

C interpreted the treachery to refer to a “beef” between Jones, Hadley and radio station management.

He said he had not made the allegations public at that time, and said if he had wanted to damage the broadcaster he could have made it public.

Bashir told the court in her opening that “rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case”.

Complainant C has finished his evidence and the trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues on Friday with witnesses who are relevant to his allegations.

australia.title: More than 1,000 birds found dead in three mass mortality events amid ‘significant’ H5 escalation in Australia
australia.snippet: South Australian premier Peter Malinauskas says there have still been no detections in poultry or livestock and no mass deaths involving ...
australia.content:
The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, has declared a “significant escalation” in H5 bird flu in the state after the detection of three mass mortality events involving more than 1,000 greater crested terns.

Malinauskas said the cause of the deaths was presumed to be H5 bird flu.

State authorities were also investigating a suspected case in a little penguin found on Kangaroo Island, with the premier telling the state parliament the development was of “particular concern”.

Separately, the Tasmanian government said it was investigating 28 little penguin deaths on King Island with testing under way to determine whether the birds died of H5 bird flu.

Malinauskas said aerial surveillance on Wednesday detected the three mass mortality events in South Australia, all on offshore islands where H5 bird flu had been detected in recent weeks.

He said more than 1,000 dead crested terns were found across Troubridge Island off the Yorke Peninsula and the Pages Islands – known as North Page and South Page – off Kangaroo Island.

The deaths would represent the biggest detected mass casualty events from suspected H5 bird flu since the deadly strain arrived on the Australian mainland in June.

Greater crested terns, a common Australian seabird, have been the most affected local species so far.

The Pages Islands are a known breeding site for a colony of endangered Australian sea lions and long-nosed fur seals are known to visit the islands.

Troubridge Island conservation park is an important breeding area for birds and home to a large colony of little penguins, as well as black cormorants and many crested terns.

Malinauskas said the state’s aerial patrols, involving helicopters, planes and drones with support from field crews, were not limited to coastal sea birds. He said crews also looked for mammals, such as Australian sea lions or long-nosed fur seals, which might be affected by H5 bird flu.

“Fortunately, so far, no mass mortality event … involving mammals has yet been detected or reported,” he said.

He said there remained no detections in poultry or livestock.

At a later media conference, the government said new cases in greater crested terns had also been detected in Flagstaff Hill, McLaren Vale, North Haven in the Adelaide area, Lucky Bay on the Eyre Peninsula and Tanunda in the Barossa region.

South Australia’s first confirmed case in a raven had also been detected at Port MacDonnell on the Limestone Coast.

Georgie Cornish, executive director of biosecurity at the department of primary industries and regions, said the detection in the Barossa illustrates the “movement [of H5 bird flu] from coast inwards”.

Malinauskas said the state would continue to take “every practical and appropriate action available” to protect South Australia’s wildlife, industries and communities.

He told the parliament that broad-scale vaccination of wild birds was “neither practical nor appropriate”, but said the state was considering “targeted vaccination of selected captive and managed populations of our most threatened native birds, where it is safe, feasible and likely to provide a conservation benefit”.

Late on Friday, the New South Wales government also confirmed H5 bird flu in seven birds found at Narooma and Merimbula on the state’s south coast. Six of the birds were greater crested terns and one a giant petrel. The government said it was “progressing plans to vaccinate priority captive native species”, including regent honeyeaters and little penguins.

In Tasmania, the state government said aerial surveillance on Wednesday spotted 28 dead little penguins and three dead crested terns at the Port of Grassy on King Island.

The Department of Natural Resources and Environment said samples had been collected and sent for laboratory testing for H5 bird flu, with results expected “during the week”.

“Tasmanians care deeply about our wildlife, and particularly our penguins, so we understand that reports like these may be distressing for the community,” a spokesperson said.

They said staff planned to collect the dead birds on Thursday to reduce the risk of transmission.

The body of missing 18-year-old bushwalker Lily Hooper has been found in a remote New South Wales national park more than a week after she set out on her hike.

Initially, police media reported a “hiker” had been found after the multi-agency search in the rugged terrain of Nattai national park, about 90km south-west of Sydney.

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, had told parliament she’d been “found alive” with half a bottle of water, but within minutes he announced: “I’ve got some terrible news. I apologise … it seems as if the earlier advice was wrong.”

The police assistant commissioner Joe Cassar told reporters: “There’s no playbook to communication.”

world.title: More than 100 dead after goldmine collapses in Central African Republic
world.snippet: The collapse was caused by a landslide, while local officials say the death toll is likely to rise as recovery efforts continue More than...
world.content:
More than 100 people have died after an artisanal goldmine at a small village in western Central African Republic (CAR) caved in due to a landslide, local officials and aid workers said on Wednesday.

The landslide happened on Tuesday afternoon in the village of Zamboye, about 50km (31 miles) from the town of Baboua and close to the border of Cameroon. Footage on social media appeared to show an avalanche of sand descend on a group of people, likely the miners, and cover them.

A statement by a local public prosecutor said many others were trapped under the deluge. It did not mention the number of fatalities. However, Gervais Ganagoroh, a Red Cross volunteer involved in the relief effort, told the Associated Press news agency on Wednesday that more than 100 bodies had been recovered from the collapse and ⁠a senior official at a local mining association confirmed that number to Reuters.

Local media in CAR reported that authorities had launched an investigation into the incident. A second prosecutor from Baboua told the press that the incident is believed to have been caused by “the collapse of several underground tunnels in which miners were operating”.

“The ground completely collapsed and buried people,” Cedric Mbango, a miner at the site, told the AFP news agency, describing the incident as “catastrophic”.

Rescuers are racing to retrieve the bodies of victims and find survivors among the miners, believed to be nationals of CAR and Cameroon. Authorities in Cameroon’s Eastern region said at least three of its citizens have been identified as victims in the incident.

Grégoire Mvongo, the region’s governor told state-owned radio on Wednesday that he was “working in close collaboration with our Central African colleagues to deal with the aftermath of this tragedy”.

Bertrand Be Yangué, a member of the Zamboye youth council, said that “finding them alive would be a miracle.” He added: “We are saddened and heartbroken to see young men and women perish after coming to the mines to save their families from despair.”

The toll is expected to rise as the rescue efforts continue, added Yangué.

The Central African news website Corbeau News reported that heavy machinery, including tractors, was being used in the retrieval mission and could jeopardise the rescue of those still alive under the landmass.

The exact number of people who were in the mine at the time of the cave-in remains unknown.

Small scale artisanal mines are common in different parts of Africa, despite regulations criminalising them, as unemployment continues to drive able-bodied men to abandoned or unused mines, to eke a living. The mining sites often operate with weak safety standards leading to repeated incidents: at least 40 people have died in several mining incidents in CAR this year alone.

world.title: Five Americans among seven killed in safari helicopter crash in Kenya
world.snippet: Officials say all seven people onboard killed, including Telemundo executive and Ecuador intelligence chief Seven people, including five ...
world.content:
Seven people, including five Americans, were killed when a safari helicopter crashed on Wednesday morning in a remote part of northern Kenya, according to local police and the state department.

Among the dead were an executive with Telemundo, the US-based Spanish-language network owned by NBC Universal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service.

The helicopter crashed at 9.13am while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu county, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement that an investigation was under way. It said there were seven people onboard – six passengers and the pilot.

Late on Wednesday, David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters that all seven people onboard had died.

In Washington, the state department said five of those killed were US citizens. “The US embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” it said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.”

The identities of the victims were not revealed but a local television station in Miami, Florida, said that José Suárez, 55, president and GM of several Telemundo stations in Florida, was among those killed.

“We are heartbroken to learn the tragic news that José was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya,” the NBC affiliate in Miami quoted from a joint statement from NBC Universal and Telemundo leadership.

The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with the travel company +Beyond.

Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.

Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.

The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.

Ecuador confirmed later on Wednesday that Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of the country’s national intelligence center, died in the helicopter crash in Kenya.

In a statement posted on X, the presidency said: “In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates.”

Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist with his wife, Stephany Hollihan Vasconez, who also died in the crash. She was a US and Ecuadorian citizen. They are survived by their two children.

Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a thriving tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe.

In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.

world.title: Spain to allow 500 children in Ceuta to go to mainland in immigration U-turn
world.snippet: Madrid government changes stance after previously saying anyone who entered territory illegally would be sent back Europe live – latest u...
world.content:
The Spanish government has U-turned and said it will allow 500 migrant children in Ceuta to relocate to the mainland.

The majority of the estimated 70,000 people who crossed into Ceuta – a Spanish territory on the coast of north Africa – on 30 July have returned to Morocco. However, under Spanish law, the state has a duty of care to young, unaccompanied migrants until they reach the age of 18.

On 13 August, the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, had said: “Anyone who illegally enters Ceuta or Melilla [another Spanish enclave in north Africa] knows they will be sent back because Spain and Morocco work together to this end. They will not reach the peninsula, nor the European continent and nor will they remain indefinitely in Ceuta or Melilla.”

The transfer of the children to the Spanish mainland is a sensitive political topic as several regions governed jointly by the conservative People’s party and the far-right Vox are reluctant or opposed to receiving their quota.

To minimise conflict, the youth ministry, in coordination with the Ceuta government, is devising an urgent plan under which NGOs and child protection agencies take charge of the most vulnerable children, girls in particular, without transferring their guardianship to Spain’s regional governments.

Rubén Pérez Correa, the secretary of state for children, has been in Ceuta since Sunday in an effort to resolve a situation in which hundreds of children are living on the street and existing on handouts from Ceuta residents.

News of the government’s plan came only hours after the European Commission said that under EU law all of the migrants should be returned to Morocco. Asked to clarify, the commission’s spokesperson on internal affairs, Markus Lammert, said that by law all irregular migrants remaining in Ceuta should be sent back, “including unaccompanied minors”.

The People’s party has rejected the government plan, saying the best place for the children is with their families. “If Morocco has asked for the children to be returned and if Europe says the illegal immigrants should all be returned, whether children or not, what more does the government need?” the People’s party deputy finance spokesperson, Juan Bravo, said in a television interview.

The mixed messages partly derive from the fact the latest European pact on immigration has not yet been incorporated into Spanish law and therefore Spain’s own legislation on the treatment of unaccompanied minors remains in force.

According to Spain’s ministry of inclusion and migration, as of last March 21,104 people aged 16-23 were guardians of the state, of whom about 3,500 were under 17. Approximately 50% were from Morocco. Girls made up about 8% of the total.

world.title: Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo now deadliest in country’s history
world.snippet: At least 2,325 people have died from the virus, according to official data, with outbreak on track to be biggest in history The Ebola out...
world.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is now the deadliest in the country’s history, with at least 2,325 people dead, according to government data, surpassing the toll from the 2018-20 outbreak.

The DRC’s public health institute said confirmed cases had risen to 4,945, including 101 detected in the previous 24 hours.

The World Health Organization has said the outbreak is on track to surpass west Africa’s 2014-16 Ebola outbreak as the biggest in history. The 2014-16 outbreak resulted in 28,616 cases and 11,325 deaths across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to WHO data.

On Friday, the UN said Ebola “is winning in the Democratic Republic of the Congo” and said the epidemic was killing one person every 30 minutes.

Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.

The latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in the DRC have made this outbreak – the 17th in the country’s history – the fastest-growing in the known history of the virus. It took almost five months for the 2014-16 west Africa outbreak to reach 1,000 deaths, compared with more than 2,000 deaths in less than three months in this outbreak.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments yet for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current surge in cases. Nonetheless, 1,000 people in the DRC have recovered from the infection, with 730 still in healthcare or isolation facilities.

Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the strain began last month in Ituri. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said last week that two vaccines developed specifically for Bundibugyo were now being tested on people.

Thomas Parisch, a public health specialist recently deployed to the DRC with Médecins Sans Frontières, said: “Normally, as an outbreak progresses, the case fatality ratio should fall as contact tracing improves and patients are identified and treated earlier. Instead, we’re still seeing many cases detected very late, when treatment is less likely to succeed, with many identified only after they die in the community.”

Uganda has reported at least 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case reported there was on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded. The government declared the country Ebola-free on 28 July after the last Ebola patient, a Congolese national, was discharged on 16 July.

In May, the WHO declared the outbreak in the DRC and Uganda as a public health emergency of international concern. It said sequencing showed the outbreak had started months earlier, in February.

Ebola is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other body fluids of infected people, including dead bodies, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to the WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.

The response to this outbreak has been hampered by attacks on healthcare facilities, often fuelled by misinformation about safe burial practices, as well as strikes by some unpaid health workers. Decades of unrest and outside interference on traumatised communities, as well as poor health and road infrastructure have also complicated the picture.

More than 70% of people die in the community and not in health centres, said Mohamed Janabi, the WHO’s regional Africa director.

Jean-Paul Malo Lotsima, a civil society official in the Djugu area of Ituri, told the AFP news agency: “People prefer to be treated at home, thinking it is a case of poisoning or some other illness.”

He added: “It’s often at the last minute, when the family realises that the situation is getting worse, that patients are taken to hospital. And sometimes, they die on the way.”

Flavier Ngurima, who lives in Nizi, one of the hotspots of the outbreak in Ituri, said his brother died before reaching the treatment centre. “We had called on a nurse from the family to treat him at home because the patient and the family members were afraid to go to the ETC [treatment centre],” he said. “They said that over there, a lot of people die.”

world.title: Zimbabwe boat accident death toll hits 68 as 22 more bodies recovered
world.snippet: Eighteen children among the people killed after ferry capsized on Lake Kariba Twenty-two more bodies have been recovered after a boat acc...
world.content:
Twenty-two more bodies have been recovered after a boat accident in Zimbabwe, taking the death toll to 68, police said on Saturday.

The ferry capsized on Tuesday on Lake Kariba, on the border with Zambia. An investigation has suggested it was overloaded when it turned over during heavy winds.

Eighteen children were among the people killed, Zimbabwe’s police said, in what is believed to be the country’s deadliest such disaster.

Most of the passengers are believed to be villagers and fish traders who lived around the lake.

Officials said the vessel was authorised to carry 90 people but was packed with 114 adults, five crew members and an unspecified number of children.

Lt Col Joseph Muchechesi, commander of the boat regiment involved in the search operation, said: “So far today we have managed to take 22 bodies. We are confident that we will manage to retrieve all the bodies.”

The civil protection unit said on Wednesday that 77 people had been rescued.

Hundreds of people gathered at the district hospital in the lakeside town of Kariba to identify the bodies of their relatives and loved ones.

A public memorial service was held in Kariba, nearly 280km (175 miles) north-west of the capital Harare, on Thursday before the burials started.

Survivors said they pleaded with the ferry driver to turn back as the vessel had begun taking on water soon after departing.

Chance Siyamavhu, 45, told Agence France-Presse: “Thank God that a wave pushed the sinking vessel and we managed to climb on top.

“When the boat capsized, most of the people scrambled to get the lifejackets but most of them did not even know how to use them.

“Most people could not make it.”

Lake Kariba is the world’s largest manmade lake by volume. It stretches more than 200km (124 miles) and is up to 40km (25 miles) wide in places.

It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people.

In 2014, 26 people, 24 of them children, drowned in Zambia’s part of the lake, when the boat meant to transport them to independence day celebrations capsized.

On the Zimbabwean side, five passengers drowned in a 2021 incident.
